The `lpplsF` package: A guided tour

Fitting, diagnostics and Lagrange regularization for the LPPLS bubble model

lpplsF

2026-10-31

Source: vignettes/articles/lpplsF_guide.Rmd
lpplsF_guide.Rmd

lpplsF fits the log-periodic power-law singularity (LPPLS) model of Sornette and co-authors — a model of the faster-than-exponential, log-periodically decorated price growth that can precede a financial-bubble crash. This document is a guided tour of the package: every calibration, diagnostic and plot it offers, worked through on a series of examples that build on one another.

How to read it. Each section builds on the previous one, from a single calibration on simulated data, through the optimizer’s behaviour and its sensitivity to noise, to rolling-window bubble-onset detection and finally a real market series. You can read it front to back, or jump to the section matching the function you need.

Theory, and where to find it. This guide is about using the package; it assumes the model rather than deriving it. The accompanying master’s thesis sets out the theory behind every method used here: the model’s derivation, the calibration scheme, the modified profile likelihood and the Lagrange regularization. Each section below names the thesis figure it corresponds to, so you can read the two side by side.

Reproducibility. The single-model calibrations run live every time the document is knitted. The multi-fit noise and rolling-window tables (tens of minutes to hours of CPU) are shipped precomputed and loaded instead. The specification for each is given in its own section (see Reproducibility and the cache), and the dual-regime rolling calibration can be re-run in place by knitting with

rmarkdown::render("lpplsF_guide.Rmd", params = list(recompute = TRUE))

Interactive surfaces. The SSE landscapes are interactive plotly surfaces (drag to rotate). sse_surface_plot(..., static = TRUE) draws the same grids as static base-R persp() surfaces, which is how the package’s PDF overview, vignette("lpplsF"), shows them.

The model and its calibration landscape

The core generator is eval_lppls(). A single LPPLS trajectory is a deterministic function of a critical time \(t_c\), the power-law exponent \(m\), the log-periodic angular frequency \(\omega\), and linear coefficients \(A, B, C_1, C_2\):

## ten points spread across a series whose critical time is tc = 1001
round(eval_lppls(seq(1, 1000, length.out = 10),
                 A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                 tc = 1001, m = 0.6, omega = 8), 4)
##  [1] 6.3886 6.4297 6.5710 6.7978 6.9676 6.9962 7.1630 7.3707 7.6021 7.9765

Calibration means minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) between the model and observed log-prices over the nonlinear parameters \((t_c, m, \omega)\); the linear parameters are profiled out. Before fitting, it helps to see that SSE landscape. sse_surface_plot() evaluates the SSE over a grid of two parameters, holding the rest fixed, and draws that surface. Give the values of the parameters you are not scanning, name the two you are, and give each a range:

sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(tc = 1001, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("m", "omega"),
  span   = list(m = c(0.1, 0.9), omega = c(6, 13)),
  mode   = 0
)

Every surface in this section is produced that way. sse_contour_plot(), which it wraps, returns the grid itself and can draw a contour plot of it as well.

Simulated LPPLS(0) data

Thesis Figure 10. A single LPPLS(0) process (the Filimonov–Sornette parameterization, mode = 0) of length \(N = 1000\) plus Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 0.05\)); the SSE is evaluated on the first 910 observations (the critical time \(t_c = 1001\) lies beyond the fitting window).

\(t_c\) \(m\) \(\omega\) \(A\) \(B\) \(C_1\) \(C_2\)
1001 0.6 8 8 -0.025 0.0015 0.001 
set.seed(3630)
sigma <- 0.05
N     <- 1000
tc    <- N + 1                      # 1001
sim   <- vapply(1:N, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = tc, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))

log_p <- sim[1:910]                 # fitting window
t_obs <- (1:N)[1:910]

SSE over \(m\) and \(\omega\) — thesis Figure 10(a)

Flat/low for small \(m\), a weak depression near \(m = 0.6\), then a steep rise for larger \(m\); only small oscillating variation along \(\omega\).

SSE over \(t_c\) and \(m\) — thesis Figure 10(b)

Flat for small \(m\), rising strongly for larger \(m\); the variation along \(t_c\) is small for small \(m\).

SSE over \(t_c\) and \(\omega\) — thesis Figure 10(c)

Many strong oscillations along the \(\omega\) direction — the source of the multi-modal, hard-to-optimize likelihood that motivates the profile methods below.

Higher-order Landau variants

Thesis Figure 11. The package also implements the 1st- and 2nd-order Landau expansions (mode = 1, mode = 2). In those modes \(C_2\) plays the role of the phase \(\phi\), so a “\(\phi\) axis” is produced by scanning \(C_2\). The axes below are labelled \(\phi\) accordingly.

\(t_c\) and \(\phi\), 1st-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(a)

This surface uses the \(N = 1000\) mode-0 data from the previous section, examined under the mode-1 \((t_c, \phi)\) landscape — modes 0 and 1 are equivalent parameterizations of the same 1st-order Landau LPPL. The phase periodicity (\(2\pi\)) produces three local minima across \(\phi \in [1, 20]\), plus a boundary solution at small \(\phi\).

A 2nd-order Landau simulation

The 2nd-order model adds a pre-critical regime of length \(\Delta t = 500\) with secondary frequency \(\Delta\omega = 0\). SSE is evaluated on the first 1910 of \(N = 2000\) observations.

\(t_c\) \(m\) \(\omega\) \(A\) \(B\) \(C_1\) \(C_2\) \(\Delta t\)
2001 0.6 8 8 -0.025 0.0015 0.001 500 
set.seed(3630)
N2  <- 2000
tc2 <- N2 + 1
sim2 <- vapply(1:N2, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = tc2, m = 0.6, omega = 8, mode = 2, T1 = 500) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))
log_p2 <- sim2[1:1910]
t_obs2 <- (1:N2)[1:1910]

\(t_c\) and \(\phi\), 2nd-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(b)

Note the wider \(t_c\) axis: the pre-critical regime lets parameters wander outside the usual LPPLS filter values.

\(t_c\) and \(\omega\), 2nd-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(c)

Even more rugged than the Filimonov variant: narrow, deep ravines and strong oscillations along \(\omega\).

Fitting a single model

fit_lppls() is the workhorse. With mode = "MPL" it calibrates by modified profile likelihood: for each candidate \(t_c\) in the search window it profiles out \((m, \omega)\) (and the linear parameters), then builds a likelihood interval for \(t_c\). We calibrate two simulated series: one with Gaussian noise (M1), one with AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise (M2). Each holds out the last 200 points, fits on \([1, 1800]\), and searches \(t_c\) over \([1801, 2100]\); the true \(t_c = 2001\).

## One-row tidy estimate table from a fit_lppls() result.
est_row <- function(fit) {
  e <- fit$fit[[1]]
  data.frame(tc = e$tc, m = e$m, omega = e$omega,
             A = unname(e$A), B = unname(e$B),
             C1 = unname(e$C1), C2 = unname(e$C2), D = unname(e$D))
}

## The calibration shared by M1 and M2. fp/pp/tp ask fit_lppls() to also attach
## the fit plot, the per-tc parameter plot and the BFGS trace plot to the
## returned object, so they are available later without refitting.
fit_call <- function(log_price) {
  fit_lppls(
    log_price = log_price, fh = 300, hold_out = 200,
    lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
    tc_init = 1950, m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
    mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5), beta_method = "crossprod",
    fp = TRUE, pp = TRUE, tp = TRUE
  )
}

The Gaussian series is regenerated from set.seed(3630). The GARCH series ships with this guide as garch_series.rds: it was drawn with rugarch, whose simulated paths depend on the package version, so it is stored rather than re-simulated.

set.seed(3630)
Nf <- 2000
gauss_series <- vapply(1:Nf, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = Nf + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))
garch_series <- readRDS(dpath("garch_series.rds"))$log_p
## 300 profile-likelihood optimizations per series
fit_gauss <- fit_call(gauss_series)
fit_garch <- fit_call(garch_series)

Reading the fit: print() diagnostics

A calibration can look perfectly good as a plot and still be untrustworthy. The print() method for fit_lppls() reports the estimate together with the checks that decide whether it means anything — this is the fastest way to find out whether a fit is worth interpreting.

fit_gauss
## LPPLS calibration (mode = MPL)
##   Window:    n = 1800   fh = 300   hold_out = 200   num_searches = 1
##   Estimate:  tc = 1996.01   m = 0.6050   omega = 7.9554   D = 1.049
##              SSE = 4.24025
##   Bounds:    estimate interior;  fits at a bound: m 0/300, omega 0/300
##   Basins:    SSE 4.24025..4.88259;
##              no distinct inferior cluster (largest gap 0.02 of the spread)
##   Filters:   B out of range 0   D out of range 0
##   MPL:       defined at 300/300 tc   MPLE = 1996
##              LI(0.05) [1970, 2023]   LI(0.10) [1973, 2019]
##              LI(0.50) [1984, 2009]

Line by line:

  • Bounds. \((m, \omega)\) are optimised inside a box. If the optimum sits on a wall, the SSE is still falling in that direction and the estimate is a constrained one — the regularity conditions behind the modified profile likelihood do not hold, and its intervals mean nothing. The check is reported twice: for the point estimate, and as a count across all the per-\(t_c\) conditional fits. The second matters on its own, because an interior point estimate can still rest on a profile that is pinned nearly everywhere.
  • Basins. Each candidate \(t_c\) gets its own \((m, \omega)\) search, and with few restarts some land in a worse local optimum than others. Distance from the best SSE will not detect this — the conditional SSE should rise away from the optimal \(t_c\), so a healthy profile also has fits well above the minimum. What betrays a failed search is a gap: the sorted SSEs falling into a good cluster and a distinctly worse one. The reported number is the largest gap between consecutive sorted values as a share of the total spread, which is scale-free and near zero for a smooth profile.
  • Filters. How many candidate fits were rejected for \(B \ge 0\) or for damping, \(D\), below its floor. These are the two constraints fit_lppls() reports internally, otherwise visible only as warnings while the fit runs.
  • MPL. How much of the \(t_c\) grid the modified profile likelihood is defined on. It is NA wherever \(\det(X'X - H) \le 0\), which at a constrained optimum carries no guarantee of sign.

A Diagnostics: block of ! lines appears only when something is wrong, so a clean fit prints none — as here. The S&P 500 example shows one that prints six.

fit_garch
## LPPLS calibration (mode = MPL)
##   Window:    n = 1800   fh = 300   hold_out = 200   num_searches = 1
##   Estimate:  tc = 1979.96   m = 0.5675   omega = 7.9367   D = 0.978
##              SSE = 4.4327
##   Bounds:    estimate interior;  fits at a bound: m 0/300, omega 0/300
##   Basins:    SSE 4.4327..5.62348;
##              no distinct inferior cluster (largest gap 0.01 of the spread)
##   Filters:   B out of range 0   D out of range 0
##   MPL:       defined at 300/300 tc   MPLE = 1980
##              LI(0.05) [1957, 2004]   LI(0.10) [1959, 2001]
##              LI(0.50) [1969, 1991]

Per-\(t_c\) parameter estimates — thesis Figure 14

Passing pp = TRUE to fit_lppls() attaches a parameter plot: each estimated parameter (and the objective) as a function of the candidate \(t_c\), with the objective minimum (\(\hat t_c\)) marked. \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) trace near-sinusoidal curves that distort far from the true \(t_c\) — more so under GARCH noise. No extra calibration runs; these reuse the fits above.

M1 — Gaussian noise — thesis Figure 14(a) 

fit_gauss$param_plot

M2 — AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise — thesis Figure 14(b) 

fit_garch$param_plot

Reading the optimizer: BFGS traces

Thesis Figure 15. With tp = TRUE, fit_lppls() attaches a trace plot. It shows the SSE landscape over \((m, \omega)\) at the estimated \(t_c\), overlaid with the BFGS path — red dot at the start \((m_{\text{init}}, \omega_{\text{init}}) = (0.2, 12)\), green diamond at the estimate.

\(B\) and the damping \(D\) are not search coordinates. At every point of the landscape they follow from the least-squares solution for the linear parameters, so the plot shows them as regions instead: shaded where that solution would be out of range, black for \(B \ge 0\) and white for \(D\) below its floor of 0.8, each edged with a dashed line. The conditions are checked only where a search ends, so a path may cross a shaded region on its way.

\((m, \omega)\) topology — thesis Figure 15

The governing topology for calibration: a single interior minimum BFGS finds easily. The GARCH minimum sits slightly further from the true \((0.6, 8)\). In both, the white lobe at small \(m\) is where the damping would fall below 0.8, and the Gaussian path touches its edge on the way to the estimate. \(B\) is negative across the whole box, so nothing is shaded black.

fit_gauss$trace_plot   # Gauss

fit_garch$trace_plot   # GARCH

Robustness to noise

Thesis Figures 16, 17 and 18. How much noise can a calibration take before its estimates stop meaning anything? That is a property of the model rather than of any particular series, so it is studied on a known signal: take a deterministic LPPLS path, add noise at a range of levels, recalibrate at each, and watch the estimates move.

lppls_noise_sweep() runs that experiment. It takes the clean signal, a vector of noise levels, and the arguments to pass to fit_lppls(), and returns one row per level:

N      <- 2000
signal <- eval_lppls(seq_len(N), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                     tc = N + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8)

sweep <- lppls_noise_sweep(
  signal,
  sd_seq   = seq(0.005, 0.100, by = 0.005),      # 20 noise levels
  fit_args = list(fh = 150, hold_out = 100,
                  lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
                  upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                  m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
                  mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5)),
  seed = 3630
)

The noise argument decides what kind of perturbation is studied. It defaults to rnorm, and takes any function of n returning standardised innovations, so a heavy-tailed or serially dependent alternative can be compared against the Gaussian case on the very same signal:

## Student-t innovations, rescaled to unit variance so `sd_seq` still reads as
## a standard deviation
heavy <- function(n) rt(n, df = 4) / sqrt(4 / 2)
lppls_noise_sweep(signal, sd_seq = seq(0.005, 0.100, by = 0.005),
                  noise = heavy, fit_args = fit_args, seed = 3630)

The four sweeps below are of that shape: M1 and M2 under Gaussian noise, and the same pair under AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, where M2 is M1 with \(C_1, C_2\) negated (opposite phase). That is 80 calibrations, so the tables are shipped precomputed (noise_*.rds) and loaded here; see Reproducibility and the cache.

Parameter estimates vs noise level — thesis Figure 16

noise_param_plot() draws each estimate against the noise level, one panel per parameter. \(\omega, C_1, C_2\) (the log-periodic parameters) are the most noise-sensitive.

Gaussian noise, M1 

noise_param_plot(noise_m1_gauss)

AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, M1 

noise_param_plot(noise_m1_garch)

\(t_c\) likelihood intervals vs noise level

noise_tc_plot() draws the \(t_c\) estimate and the MPLE with the nested likelihood-interval bands. Pass true_tc on a simulated signal and it marks the true value, here \(t_c = 2001\).

Gaussian noise: M1, then M2 at opposite phase — thesis Figure 17 

noise_tc_plot(noise_m1_gauss, true_tc = 2001)

AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise: M1, then M2 at opposite phase — thesis Figure 18

Rolling windows and Lagrange regularization

Thesis Figures 21 to 23. Lagrange regularization (Demos & Sornette, 2019) tries to find the onset of a bubble by rolling the calibration start \(T_1\) forward (fixed end \(T_2\)) and looking for the window where the normalized residual \(\chi^2_{np}(T_1)\) stops falling. The package splits this into a reusable primitive and cheap post-processing:

  • lppls_rolling() runs one calibration per \(T_1\) (the expensive part);
  • lppls_lagrange(), rolling_tc_plot(), rolling_param_plot(), chi_sq_np_plot(), chi_sq_lambda_plot() are all post-processing on it.

In a pure LPPL process every window is already LPPL, so \(\chi^2_{np}\) is flat and regularization has nothing to correct. So the example is a dual-regime series consisting of a flat “ranging” segment for \(t < 600\) that switches to an LPPL process at \(t = 600\) (tc = 2001, m = 0.6, omega = 8, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001; Gaussian noise \(\sigma = 0.05\), seed 3630). The rolling approaches the onset from below: as \(T_1\) climbs toward 600 each window sheds more of the pre-LPPL data and the fit tightens, so \(\chi^2_{np}\) decreases; once \(T_1\) passes 600 the window is pure LPPL again and the trend flattens. The rolling (\(T_1 = 1 \to 1001\) step 10, \(T_2 = 1900\); 101 windows) is shipped precomputed as lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds.

## The dual-regime series: flat at the LPPL value at t = 600 for t < 600, then
## the LPPL process itself, with N(0, 0.05^2) noise throughout. In this example
## the two segments draw their noise from separate seeds: `seed` for the flat
## prefix, `seed + 1` for the bubble. So both set.seed() calls are needed to
## reproduce it. (This is not really important, it just happens to be the way
## the figures for the thesis were generated.)
N_rg <- 2000
build_rg <- function(seed, onset = 600) {
  bub <- eval_lppls(onset:N_rg, 8, -0.025, 0.0015, 0.001, N_rg + 1, 0.6, 8)
  set.seed(seed + 1)
  c(rep(bub[1], onset - 1), bub) +
    c({ set.seed(seed); rnorm(onset - 1) * 0.05 }, rnorm(N_rg - onset + 1) * 0.05)
}

## Regenerated on both paths: it is instant, and the residual guard below needs
## the series even when the calibration comes from the cache.
lp_rg <- build_rg(3630)
## 101 windows, each a 150-candidate tc scan (MPL: the likelihood
## intervals rolling_tc_plot() needs).
roll_rg <- lppls_rolling(
  lp_rg,
  t1_seq = seq(1, 1001, by = 10),
  hold_out = 100,
  fh = 150,
  fit_args = list(
    lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
    upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
    m_init = 0.2,
    o_init = 12,
    num_searches = 1,
    mode = "MPL",
    mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5),
    factr = 1e7)
  )
lag_rg <- lppls_lagrange(roll_rg, p = 0)
lag_rg
## LPPLS Lagrange regularization
##   Windows (T1):  101  (from 1 to 1001)
##   T2 (cal. end): 1900
##   p (denominator correction): 0
##   Trend: chi^2_np = 0.0054087 + (-3.9517e-06) * T1
##   lambda* = -beta1 = 3.9517e-06
##   Optimal T1* = 501

Optimal \(T_1^* =\) 501 (true onset 600); \(\lambda =\) 3.95^{-6} \(> 0\) — a genuine bias trend (a pure LPPL series would give \(\lambda \approx 0\)).

lppls_rolling() keeps the fit from every window. To examine the one that Lagrange regularization selected, locate it in the sequence and pull out the quantities that describe it.

k_rg  <- which(roll_rg$t1_seq == lag_rg$t1_star)  # position of the optimal window
T1_rg <- roll_rg$t1_seq[k_rg]                     # its calibration start, T1*
nc_rg <- roll_rg$table$n_cal[k_rg]                # how many points it calibrated on
T2_rg <- T1_rg + nc_rg - 1                        # its calibration end, T2
f_rg  <- roll_rg$fits[[k_rg]]                     # the fit itself

The generated series and its fit — thesis Figure 21

Blue the generated series, red the fitted LPPLS process up to \(\hat t_c\), dashed markers at the calibration bounds and \(\hat t_c\). The series spans two regimes and the fit is calibrated on only the later part, so the red curve starts at \(T_1^*\) — the flat regime is shown but never fitted. lppls_rolling() stores the fit in window-local time (\(t = 1\) at \(T_1\)), so \(\hat t_c\) is shifted by the window offset to draw it on the global clock.

f_glob    <- f_rg
f_glob$tc <- f_rg$tc + (T1_rg - 1)   # window-local -> global clock

fit_plot(f_glob, seq_along(lp_rg), lp_rg, T1 = T1_rg, T2 = T2_rg)

Give fit_plot() both window bounds and it draws the curve only where the fit applies.

Rolling-\(T_1\) estimates — thesis Figure 22

How the \(t_c\) estimate and the six parameters move as \(T_1\) rolls across the onset. For \(T_1\) well below 600 the window still contains ranging data and the estimates wander; as \(T_1\) approaches and passes 600 the window becomes predominantly, then purely, LPPL and \(\hat t_c\) settles near the true 2001.

rolling_tc_plot(roll_rg)

rolling_param_plot(roll_rg)

Lagrange regularization — thesis Figure 23

\(\chi^2_{np}(T_1)\) with the OLS bias trend (red), then the regularized objective \(\chi^2_{\lambda^*}(T_1)\) with the optimal \(T_1^*\) (green):

chi_sq_np_plot(lag_rg)

chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag_rg)

Is that decrease real, or a noise artifact? That question, and the autocorrelation-robust lr_trend_test() that answers it, are taken up in a separate investigation, lagrange_inference_report.Rmd, in the package’s misc/ directory on GitHub. It is not built with the package.

Residuals at \(T_1^*\)

The residual QQ plot for the window at \(T_1^*\). The residuals are near-normal.

residual_qq_plot(res_rg)

Empirical example: the S&P 500

Thesis Figures 25 to 30. The package ships the S&P 500 series as the dataset spx (see ?spx), covering exactly the calibrated window, 2009-05-18 to 2020-12-31. We fit on \([1, 2428]\) (to 2019-01-08) with hold_out = 500, fh = 500.

## `spx` is lazy-loaded with the package: 2,928 daily closes, 2009-05-18..2020-12-31.
df_spx <- data.frame(Date = spx$date, logpris = log(spx$close))
df_spx$ID <- seq_len(nrow(df_spx))
n_cal_spx <- nrow(df_spx) - 500    # 2428

A note on the series. The thesis calibrated the CRSP S&P 500 Composite series (spindx, obtained through Wharton Research Data Services). That data is licensed and cannot be redistributed, so the package ships the corresponding Yahoo Finance series (^GSPC) for the same trading days. The two agree to 1.6e-07 on average, and recalibrating on the shipped series leaves every quantity reported below unchanged: \(\hat t_c = 2717\) (2020-03-03), \(m = 0.9\), \(\omega = 6.1596\), and all three likelihood intervals identical. Only the Brent-refined \(t_c\) at the final step of the MPL computation moves, in its seventh decimal. That step refines thesis equation 38 at the \((\hat m, \hat\omega)\) which minimise equation 39 on the integer grid.

## fh = 500 profile-likelihood optimizations
spx_fit <- fit_lppls(
  log_price = df_spx$logpris, fh = 500, hold_out = 500,
  lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
  tc_init = n_cal_spx + 250, m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
  mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5),
  dates = df_spx$Date,          # calendar labels for the 1..n index
  style = "empirical",          # grey data; the forecast past T2 in red
  fp = TRUE, mpl_plot = TRUE, tp = TRUE, pp = TRUE)
e <- spx_fit$fit[[1]]

The point estimate: PLE \(t_c =\) 2020-03-03, with \(m =\) 0.9 (pinned at the upper boundary) and \(\omega =\) 6.16.

What print() says about this one

Reading the fit introduced the diagnostics on a healthy calibration, which printed no warnings. This is the contrasting case, and it is worth reading before any of the figures below:

spx_fit
## LPPLS calibration (mode = MPL)
##   Window:    n = 2428   fh = 500   hold_out = 500   num_searches = 1
##   Estimate:  tc = 2717.01 (2020-03-03)   m = 0.9000   omega = 6.1596   D = 1.545
##              SSE = 5.28678
##   Bounds:    estimate m at a bound;  fits at a bound: m 500/500, omega 169/500
##   Basins:    SSE 5.28678..8.88078;  largest gap 0.56 of the spread splits off
##              394/500 conditional fits (79%)
##   Filters:   B out of range 0   D out of range 0
##   MPL:       defined at 455/500 tc   MPLE = 2717 (2020-03-03)
##              LI(0.05) [2696, 2757]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-29)
##              LI(0.10) [2696, 2757]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-29)
##              LI(0.50) [2696, 2744]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-09)
## 
##   Diagnostics:
##     ! m pinned at an optimisation bound - a boundary solution, so the modified
##       profile likelihood and its intervals are unreliable
##     ! 394 of 500 conditional fits (79%) sit in a distinct inferior basin (SSE >=
##       7.99365 against a best of 5.28678) - raise num_searches
##     ! MPL undefined at 45 of 500 tc (det(X'X - H) <= 0 there)
##     ! LI(0.05) spans 62 grid points but only 58 are above its cutoff - range()
##       bridges 4 that are not in the interval
##     ! LI(0.10) spans 62 grid points but only 58 are above its cutoff - range()
##       bridges 4 that are not in the interval
##     ! every tc inside an interval is a good-basin fit - the interval traces
##       where the search succeeded, not the curvature of the likelihood

Six flags, and every caveat in the rest of this section follows from them. The estimate is a boundary solution, and not marginally — \(m\) is at its upper bound in the point estimate and in every conditional fit, with \(\partial\,\mathrm{SSE}/\partial m < 0\) there, so the constraint is genuinely active and the regularity conditions behind the modified profile likelihood do not hold. Most of the conditional fits sit in a distinctly inferior basin, which is why the MPL curve below is two-tiered rather than smooth, and why num_searches = 1 is the wrong setting for this series. And the MPL is undefined on part of the grid, so the curve has gaps the likelihood intervals cannot see across.

The last three are about the likelihood intervals themselves. LI(0.05) and LI(0.10) each bridge grid points that are not above their cutoff, and every \(t_c\) inside an interval is a good-basin fit, so the intervals trace where the search succeeded rather than the curvature of the likelihood. The modified profile likelihood below takes this up.

None of this is visible in the point estimate, which looks entirely ordinary.

It would be easy to read the warnings above as a defect in the data, in the settings, or in the package, and to go looking for a configuration that silences them. That would be the wrong lesson. Boundary solutions, split basins and an undefined modified profile likelihood are properties of the LPPLS model itself: the objective is non-convex, the log-periodic parameters are only weakly identified, and the regularity conditions the modified profile likelihood assumes are not guaranteed to hold at a constrained optimum.

The master’s thesis for which this package was written takes up exactly this question: When an LPPLS calibration is worth believing, and what to do when it is not. The S&P 500 case above is its Chapter 9.

Fit plot — thesis Figure 25

Because the calibration was given dates, the attached $fit_plot is already drawn on a calendar axis. Pass dates to [fit_lppls()] and every plot and printout it produces speaks in dates; omit it and everything falls back to the 1..n time index.

It was also given style = "empirical". An observed price series is given and cannot be otherwise, so it is drawn in grey, and the fitted curve splits at \(T_2\): blue where data supports it, red beyond, where the curve is a forecast. The default style = "simulated" draws a generated series in colour with a single fitted line, which is what the earlier sections use.

plot(spx_fit, "fit")

The same plot can be drawn from a bare estimate with fit_plot(), which takes dates directly:

fit_plot(spx_fit$fit[[1]], seq_len(nrow(df_spx)), df_spx$logpris,
         T2 = n_cal_spx, dates = df_spx$Date, style = "empirical")

Modified profile likelihood — thesis Figure 26

The MPLE coincides with the PLE, at 2020-03-03. The MPL: line of the printout above gives that date next to the index, and each likelihood interval in both forms. The modified profile likelihood is NA wherever \(\det(X'X - H) \le 0\). At a constrained optimum that determinant carries no guarantee of sign, which is why the same line counted gaps in the grid.

Diagnostic caveat. The point estimate agrees with the PLE, but the bands are not inference — the Bounds: and Basins: lines above already say why. Two consequences the printed summary does not spell out. First, the basin split is what makes the curve two-tiered rather than smooth: the two tiers are \(\approx 500\) log-likelihood units apart, so the plot below is not one curve but two.

Second, and the reason to distrust the bands specifically: the likelihood intervals here trace where the optimiser succeeded, not the curvature of the likelihood. Every grid point inside LI_05 is a good-basin fit and every point outside it is not; its lower edge is exactly where the good-basin run containing the PLE begins, and its upper edge is the end of the next such run, which range() bridges across the gap between them. LI_05 and LI_10 coincide for the same reason. The relative-scale plot below makes this visible: only LI_50 has a crossing. Read the MPLE, not the bands.

spx_fit$mpl_plot

The same curve on a relative scale

The absolute level of the log MPL carries no information. Its magnitude comes almost entirely from the variance term of the modified profile likelihood (thesis eq. 53), \(-\tfrac{n - p - 2}{2}\log \hat{s}_{t_c}\). A well-fitting model has a small residual variance, here \(\hat{s} = \sigma^2 \approx 0.0022\), whose logarithm is large and negative. Multiplying by \(-(n - p - 2)/2 \approx -1210\) flips the sign and scales it by the sample size, which gives \(\approx 7417\). The determinant ratio contributes only \(\approx -34\), so the curve peaks near \(7383\). The formula also drops additive constants that do not depend on \(t_c\). What the likelihood intervals actually test is the difference \(R = \log\mathrm{MPL} - \max\log\mathrm{MPL}\) against \(\log(\text{cutoff})\), and the fit already stores it as mpl_output$R.

Plotting \(R\) and restricting the view to the band the cutoffs live in provides a better view of the optimum. plot(fit, "mpl_relative") draws that view from the stored mpl_output, so it needs nothing requested at fit time. The horizontal lines are the cutoffs themselves, so each interval can be read off where the curve crosses one.

plot(spx_fit, "mpl_relative")

Only LI_50 has a crossing: the curve descends from the peak to about \(-1.15\) and then stops, so it never reaches \(\log 0.10\) or \(\log 0.05\). Those two intervals end where the good basin ends.

The rest of the diagnostics

print() is the quick triage. Three further tools answer the questions it raises: where the basins are, whether the estimate sits at a genuine minimum, and whether the intervals are closed by the likelihood or by the grid.

The basin split, drawn

plot(fit, "basin") shows every conditional fit’s SSE against its \(t_c\), split at the gap print() reported. It needs nothing that was not already computed, so it works even on a fit that requested no plots.

plot(spx_fit, "basin")

The same view of the well-behaved calibration from Fitting a single model, for contrast — one cloud, rising smoothly away from the optimal \(t_c\), which is what a profile should look like:

plot(fit_gauss, "basin")

What the basins are made of

The view above shows that the fits split, but not what they split on. "param_basin" applies the same division to every estimated parameter rather than only the objective, which is where the mechanism becomes visible.

plot(spx_fit, "param_basin")

## The split is the one summary() reports; here it is per parameter.
cut_at <- summary(spx_fit)$split_at[1]
pt     <- spx_fit$fit[[2]]
pt$basin <- ifelse(pt$value <= cut_at, "good", "inferior")
rng <- function(z) sprintf("%.3f - %.3f", min(z), max(z))
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(cbind(m, omega, D) ~ basin, data = pt, FUN = rng),
  caption = "Range of each nonlinear estimate within each basin.")
Range of each nonlinear estimate within each basin.
basin m omega D
good 0.900 - 0.900 6.000 - 6.392 1.412 - 1.548
inferior 0.900 - 0.900 10.251 - 13.000 2.363 - 3.365

The two basins are separated almost entirely by \(\omega\): The good one sits near the bottom of the \([6, 13]\) search box, the inferior one near the top. \(m\) is at \(0.9\) in both, so it plays no part in the split at all.

That separates two failures which the SSE view alone runs together. The pinned \(m\) is a boundary problem, and it affects every fit on the grid. The two tiers are an \(\omega\) multimodality problem, and it affects only which optimum a single L-BFGS-B start happens to reach — a num_searches setting, not a property of the data. The C1/C2 facets tell the same story: The inferior fits oscillate through a high-frequency regime while the good ones trace a smooth low-frequency arc.

Curvature at the estimate

The modified profile likelihood assumes the estimate is an interior minimum: Its correction uses \(\det(X'X - H)\), the observed information, which is only guaranteed positive at an interior stationary point. \(X\) holds the model’s first derivatives with respect to the six parameters, and \(H\) its second derivatives, each weighted by the residual at that observation and summed (thesis eq. 55). \(H\) is thus a residual-weighted curvature term rather than a Hessian in its own right. lppls_curvature() tests the determinant directly, and factorises it to show where the sign comes from.

By the Schur complement, \(\det(X'X - H)\) factorises into the determinant of the linear-parameter block times the determinant of the \(2 \times 2\) Hessian of the \((m, \omega)\) profile. The model is linear in \(A, B, C_1, C_2\), so their second derivatives vanish, \(H\) contributes nothing to the linear block, and what remains there is a crossproduct with a positive determinant. The sign is therefore decided entirely by curvature in the two nonlinear parameters: the \(2 \times 2\) block the function reports.

lppls_curvature(spx_fit)
## LPPLS curvature at the estimate
##   tc = 2717.01   n = 2428
##   det(X'X - H)          = +6.5784e+29   (MPL is defined only where this is > 0)
##   det(linear block)     = +1.5668e+29   (positive by construction)
##   det(profile Hessian)  = +4.1986e+00   (sets the sign above)
##   eigenvalues (m, omega): +7.5551e+00   +5.5573e-01
##   => profile Hessian is positive definite: the curvature condition behind the
##      MPL holds
##   note: m sits at an optimisation bound, so the estimate is a constrained one -
##         the gradient need not vanish there, whatever the curvature says

Read the classification and the bound note as two separate facts. The curvature is positive definite here, so the \(t_c\) the MPL reports is not an artefact of a degenerate Hessian. But \(m\) rests on its bound, so the gradient need not vanish: the estimate is a constrained one whatever the curvature says. It is the combination of sound curvature and an active constraint that makes the point estimate usable and the intervals not.

Everything at once: summary()

summary() returns the diagnostics as values rather than text, so they can be tested against instead of parsed. Printing it gives the print() report plus the curvature line and an interval breakdown.

s <- summary(spx_fit)
s$basin_gap
## [1] 0.5611065
s$mpl$li_check[[1]]
## $cutoff
## [1] 0.05
## 
## $n_in
## [1] 58
## 
## $span
## [1] 62
## 
## $contiguous
## [1] FALSE
## 
## $bridged
## [1] 4
## 
## $all_good_basin
## [1] TRUE

That last list is the interval integrity check. fit_lppls() forms each interval as range() of the \(t_c\) whose \(R\) exceeds \(\log(\text{cutoff})\) — and range() does not care whether that set has holes. When it does, the reported interval contains grid points that are not themselves in it:

s
## LPPLS calibration (mode = MPL)
##   Window:    n = 2428   fh = 500   hold_out = 500   num_searches = 1
##   Estimate:  tc = 2717.01 (2020-03-03)   m = 0.9000   omega = 6.1596   D = 1.545
##              SSE = 5.28678
##   Bounds:    estimate m at a bound;  fits at a bound: m 500/500, omega 169/500
##   Basins:    SSE 5.28678..8.88078;  largest gap 0.56 of the spread splits off
##              394/500 conditional fits (79%)
##   Filters:   B out of range 0   D out of range 0
##   MPL:       defined at 455/500 tc   MPLE = 2717 (2020-03-03)
##              LI(0.05) [2696, 2757]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-29)
##              LI(0.10) [2696, 2757]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-29)
##              LI(0.50) [2696, 2744]   (2020-01-31 .. 2020-04-09)
##   Curvature: positive definite at the estimate  (det(X'X - H) = +6.578e+29;
##              profile Hessian eigenvalues +7.555e+00, +5.557e-01)
## 
##   Diagnostics:
##     ! m pinned at an optimisation bound - a boundary solution, so the modified
##       profile likelihood and its intervals are unreliable
##     ! 394 of 500 conditional fits (79%) sit in a distinct inferior basin (SSE >=
##       7.99365 against a best of 5.28678) - raise num_searches
##     ! MPL undefined at 45 of 500 tc (det(X'X - H) <= 0 there)
##     ! LI(0.05) spans 62 grid points but only 58 are above its cutoff - range()
##       bridges 4 that are not in the interval
##     ! LI(0.10) spans 62 grid points but only 58 are above its cutoff - range()
##       bridges 4 that are not in the interval
##     ! every tc inside an interval is a good-basin fit - the interval traces
##       where the search succeeded, not the curvature of the likelihood
## 
##   Likelihood intervals:
##     LI(0.05): 58 grid points above the cutoff, interval spans 62
##               (bridges 4 points below the cutoff)
##     LI(0.10): 58 grid points above the cutoff, interval spans 62
##               (bridges 4 points below the cutoff)
##     LI(0.50): 49 grid points above the cutoff, interval spans 49  (contiguous)

LI(0.05) and LI(0.10) each span more grid points than are above their cutoff: the interval bridges the gap between two runs of good-basin fits. LI(0.50) is contiguous. This is the same conclusion the relative-scale plot above shows visually, arrived at from the numbers.

Fit diagnostics — thesis Figure 30

The BFGS path slides to the \((m, \omega)\) boundary corner; the per-\(t_c\) parameter panel shows \(m\) pinned at 0.9 with jumps where it hits the boundary.

spx_fit$trace_plot

spx_fit$param_plot

Residual QQ diagnostics — thesis Figure 27

Residuals of the SPX calibration (\(t < \hat t_c\)) against a normal and a fitted Student-t reference, both via residual_qq_plot().

residual_qq_plot(res_spx)

residual_qq_plot(res_spx, "t")

Lagrange regularization on the S&P 500 — thesis Figure 29

Rolling \(T_1 = 1 \to 501\) step 25 (21 windows), \(T_2 = 2428\) fixed; shipped precomputed as lagrange_rolling_spx.rds (21-window MPL fit). It is the spx_fit call above rolled over \(T_1\), so window 1 is spx_fit itself:

roll_spx <- lppls_rolling(
  df_spx$logpris, t1_seq = seq(1, 501, 25), hold_out = 500, fh = 500,
  fit_args = list(lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                  m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1, mode = "MPL",
                  mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5)))
roll_spx <- readRDS(dpath("lagrange_rolling_spx.rds"))
lag_spx  <- lppls_lagrange(roll_spx, p = 0)
lag_spx
## LPPLS Lagrange regularization
##   Windows (T1):  21  (from 1 to 501)
##   T2 (cal. end): 2428
##   p (denominator correction): 0
##   Trend: chi^2_np = 0.00191588 + (-1.77776e-06) * T1
##   lambda* = -beta1 = 1.77776e-06
##   Optimal T1* = 76

Optimal \(T_1^* =\) 76 (= 2009-09-02). Here \(\beta_1 < 0\), \(\lambda > 0\), so the Demos bias trend is genuinely present.

chi_sq_np_plot(lag_spx)

chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag_spx)

rolling_tc_plot(roll_spx)   # PLE saturates at the tc bound

Reproducibility and the cache

This document separates three tiers of computation:

  1. Live (always run). The SSE surfaces, all data simulation and the three single-model calibrations fit_gauss, fit_garch and spx_fit are recomputed on every knit; the calibration code is shown in full above.
  2. Cached, re-runnable in place. The dual-regime rolling calibration is cached as lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds. Knit with params = list(recompute = TRUE) to re-run it and refresh the cache.
  3. Precomputed multi-fit tables (reload-only). The 20-level noise experiments (noise_*.rds) and the S&P 500 rolling calibration (lagrange_rolling_spx.rds) are shipped precomputed. The specification for each is given in its own section, so they can be regenerated with lppls_noise_sweep() and lppls_rolling().

The only input that cannot be regenerated deterministically is the AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) series. rugarch’s simulated paths depend on the package version, so it is always loaded from garch_series.rds.
